rules.title: Do not send usage or crash data without consent
Prefer explicit opt-in for telemetry
If telemetry is on by default, announce it and make disabling easy
Disclose exactly what is collected, why, and for how long
Consider alternatives to collecting analytics
Prefer flags over positional arguments
Provide a long form for every flag
Reserve one-letter flags for frequently used options
Accept multiple arguments for the same action on many items
Avoid multiple positional arguments with different roles
Use standard flag names where a convention exists
Do not make -v ambiguous
Make the default behavior right for most users
Prompt for missing input when running interactively
Never require a prompt
Confirm before dangerous operations
Scale confirmation friction to the level of danger
Treat indirect destruction as severe
Accept - for stdin and stdout wherever a file is expected
Use a sentinel word such as none for optional flag values
Make flags and subcommands order-independent
Support standard option syntax: --flag=value, --flag value and --
Never accept secrets as flag values
Accept secrets through a file or stdin
Parse arguments with an established library
Exit zero on success and non-zero on failure
Map distinct non-zero exit codes to the important failure modes
Send primary and machine-readable output to stdout
Send logs, progress, warnings and errors to stderr
Expose per-invocation settings as flags
Accept machine- or user-specific settings via flags and environment variables
Keep project-wide settings in a version-controlled, tool-specific file
Store user config, cache, data, and state in XDG base directories
Get consent before modifying configuration owned by other programs
Prefer a drop-in file over editing a shared config file
Mark edits to shared config files with dated delimiters
Apply configuration sources in a fixed precedence order
Provide web-based documentation
Provide documentation in the terminal
Consider shipping man pages
Make terminal docs reachable through the tool itself
Distribute as a single self-contained binary where possible
Use the platform package manager when a single binary is not possible
Make uninstall easy and document it beside install instructions
Provide --version output that includes build information
Publish through the package managers your users already use
Publish checksums and signatures for release artifacts
Ship shell completions for bash, zsh, fish, and PowerShell
Install a man page or offline help with the package
Use environment variables for context-dependent behavior
Name environment variables with uppercase letters, digits, and underscores only
Keep environment variable values single-line
Do not repurpose widely used environment variable names
Honor standard general-purpose environment variables
Read project-scoped environment variables from a local .env file
Do not use .env as a substitute for a real config file
Do not accept secrets through environment variables
Catch expected errors and rewrite them for humans
Keep error output high signal and group repeated errors
Put the most important information where the user looks first
Give debug detail and bug-report instructions for unexpected errors
Make submitting a bug report effortless
Treat every user-facing surface as a stable interface
Prefer additive changes
Warn in the program before making a non-additive change
Offer a future-proof form today and stop warning once users adopt it
Treat machine-readable output as a versioned contract
Let human-readable output evolve and point scripts at stable formats
Do not use a catch-all default subcommand
Do not accept arbitrary abbreviations of subcommands or flags
Do not build in time bombs
Never block on telemetry, update checks or analytics
Version releases by the CLI contract with semantic versioning
Show full help for -h and --help, including on subcommands
Show help when -h or --help appears anywhere, ignoring other arguments
Reserve -h for help
Offer a help subcommand in git-like tools
Show concise help when required arguments are missing
Limit concise help to a description, examples, key flags and a pointer to --help
Include a support path in top-level help
Link help text to web documentation
Lead help with examples
Move exhaustive examples and tutorials out of help
List the most common flags and commands first
Format help for scanning, without leaking escape codes
Suggest a correction when input is probably a typo
Do not silently execute a guessed correction
Do not hang waiting on an interactive stdin
Prompt only when stdin is a TTY
Honor --no-input by disabling all prompts
Do not echo passwords as they are typed
Let the user escape at any time
Explain how to exit when Ctrl-C is passed through
Choose a simple, memorable, distinctive word
Use only lowercase letters, with dashes only when necessary
Keep the name short but not reserved-utility short
Make the name easy to type
Design default output for humans and detect the TTY per stream
Keep default output composable as lines of text
Provide --plain when human formatting breaks one-record-per-line
Support --json for structured output
Treat JSON output as a stable, clean contract
Print brief output on success
Offer -q to suppress non-essential output
Tell the user when state changes
Make the current state easy to inspect
Suggest the next commands to run
Make actions that cross the program's boundary explicit
Increase information density with compact, scannable formatting
Use color with intention
Disable color when not on a terminal or when the user asks
Show animations only when the stream is a terminal
Use symbols and emoji only where they add clarity
Hide developer-only information by default
Do not format stderr as a log file by default
Page long output only when interactive, with safe options
Validate input before doing any work
Respond within 100 ms
Show progress for long operations
Keep parallel work and its output coherent
Print the hidden logs when an operation fails
Put a timeout on every network operation
Make failed operations resumable by re-running them
Design for crash-only operation with atomic writes
Stay safe when many instances run at once
Expect to be scripted, run on bad networks, and used in untested environments
Exit promptly on Ctrl-C and say so immediately
Bound cleanup with a timeout
Let a second Ctrl-C skip cleanup and explain what that does
Exit with status 130 after SIGINT
Treat SIGTERM as a request for graceful shutdown
Exit quietly when the downstream pipe closes
Start correctly when a previous run skipped cleanup
Use subcommands to tame complex or closely related functionality
Share global flags, configuration and help machinery across subcommands
Use the same flag names for the same concepts in every subcommand
Keep output formatting consistent across subcommands
Pick one word order for nested subcommands and apply it everywhere
Reuse the same verbs across object types
Avoid ambiguous or similarly named subcommands
Make help <subcommand> and <subcommand> --help equivalent
Reject unknown subcommands with a suggestion
Test exit codes for success, usage errors and runtime failures
Snapshot help text and usage errors with golden files
Test output when stdout is not a TTY
Test that color opt-outs disable color
Validate JSON output against a contract
Test stdin input and the dash argument
Assert errors go to stderr and stdout stays clean
Test that non-interactive runs never prompt or hang
Test interrupt handling and cleanup
Test configuration precedence
Isolate tests from the host environment
Test the built artifact, not only internal functions
Run the suite on every target OS in CI
Test interactive behavior under a pseudo-terminal
